blocks.content: Think about your favorite food delivery app. Every time you place an order, tap Track Order, or check your bill, that hits the live production database. That database is built for one job: handle thousands of these small, fast operations per second without breaking a sweat.

Now imagine someone on the finance team asks: what was our total revenue by city for the last six months, broken down by cuisine type? That single question might have to scan every order ever placed across every city.
Run that query against the same database that's handling live orders, and you risk slowing down real checkouts for real customers just to generate a spreadsheet.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396329395-780311670.png
blocks.alt: Application traffic hitting the operational database while an ETL pipeline feeds a separate data warehouse

blocks.content: This is exactly the problem a data warehouse solves. It's a separate, structured store built specifically for these big analytical questions, so your production database never has to answer them directly.
1. Introduction
A data warehouse is a structured, curated store of data that's optimized for analytical queries and reporting. It sits apart from the transactional databases that power your actual application.
Nobody logs into the warehouse to place an order or update a profile. People query it to answer questions like how did sales trend last quarter, or which region churned the most users this month.
1.1 Why a warehouse is a different kind of database
blocks.text: 1.1 Why a warehouse is a different kind of database

blocks.content: Your production database and your warehouse might both technically be a database, but they're built for opposite jobs. One optimizes for a single record touched by one user right now. The other optimizes for millions of records scanned together to find a pattern.
["Production database: keeps the app running, one order or one profile update at a time","Data warehouse: keeps the business informed, thousands or millions of rows summarized at once"]
items: Production database: keeps the app running, one order or one profile update at a time
Data warehouse: keeps the business informed, thousands or millions of rows summarized at once

blocks.title: Same word, different job
blocks.content: Calling both of these a database is a bit like calling a bicycle and a freight train both vehicles. Technically true, but they solve very different problems.
2. OLTP versus OLAP
The two acronyms you'll hear constantly around data warehousing are OLTP and OLAP. Understanding the difference explains almost everything else in this topic.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396329396-356255513.png
blocks.alt: OLTP handling many small transactional queries side by side with OLAP running large analytical scans

blocks.content: 2.1 OLTP: the transactional world
OLTP stands for Online Transaction Processing. This is your regular application database, the one behind login, checkout, and profile updates.

["Many queries, arriving constantly","Each query touches a small number of rows, often just one","Reads and writes are both common","Speed for a single request matters more than speed for a huge scan"]
items: Many queries, arriving constantly
Each query touches a small number of rows, often just one
Reads and writes are both common
Speed for a single request matters more than speed for a huge scan

blocks.content: When you place an order, the database inserts one row into an orders table and maybe updates a row in an inventory table. That's it. Fast, small, done.
2.2 OLAP: the analytical world
OLAP stands for Online Analytical Processing. This is what a data warehouse is built for.

["Far fewer queries than OLTP, but each one is much bigger","A single query might scan millions of rows","Reads dominate. Nobody is inserting a single new order into a warehouse table by hand","The goal is aggregates and trends, not individual records"]
items: Far fewer queries than OLTP, but each one is much bigger
A single query might scan millions of rows
Reads dominate. Nobody is inserting a single new order into a warehouse table by hand
The goal is aggregates and trends, not individual records

blocks.content: A query like total revenue by region for the last quarter has to look across every sale in that window and add things up. That's an OLAP shaped question.

{"headers":["OLTP","OLAP"],"rows":[["Many small queries","Few large queries"],["Touches a handful of rows","Scans millions of rows"],["Powers the live app","Powers reports and dashboards"],["Reads and writes","Mostly reads"],["Row shaped access pattern","Column shaped access pattern"]]}

blocks.title: Same data, different shape of question
blocks.content: The interesting part is both OLTP and OLAP might ultimately be asking about the same underlying data, like orders. It's the shape of the question, one order versus a million orders, that decides which system should answer it.
3. Why you don't just query your production database
blocks.text: 3. Why you don't just query your production database

blocks.content: At this point a reasonable question is: why not skip the whole warehouse idea and just run the big analytical query against the same production database?
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396329396-33036420.png
blocks.alt: An analytical query running a full table scan alongside live application traffic on the same production database

blocks.content: Two separate problems show up if you try this.
3.1 The schema problem

Production schemas are shaped for transactions. An orders table is designed so inserting one order is fast and consistent, not so that scanning six months of orders and joining them against five other tables is convenient.
Getting a clean answer to revenue by region out of a raw OLTP schema often means joining across many normalized tables, which is slow and awkward.
3.2 The performance problem

Even if the schema could answer the question cleanly, a full table scan across millions of rows competes for the exact same CPU, memory, and disk I/O that your live users need for their fast, small requests.
Run a heavy report at the wrong moment and checkout gets slow for real customers, all so someone can look at a chart.

blocks.title: This happens more than you'd think
blocks.content: It's a common real world incident: a scheduled report or an analyst's ad hoc query saturates the production database, and the actual application slows down or times out during business hours.
4. Columnar storage: the trick that makes OLAP fast
blocks.text: 4. Columnar storage: the trick that makes OLAP fast

blocks.content: Warehouses need to scan huge numbers of rows quickly for aggregates. The technique that makes this practical is storing data by column instead of by row.
4.1 Row storage versus column storage
A normal OLTP database typically stores data row by row. All the columns for one order sit together on disk, because you usually want the whole order at once.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785397016263-59281752.png
blocks.alt: Row storage keeping full rows together compared to column storage keeping each column contiguous

blocks.content: A warehouse flips this around. It stores each column contiguously: all the order dates together, all the amounts together, all the region codes together.

Now think about total revenue by region. That query only needs the amount column and the region column. In a columnar layout, it can read just those two columns and skip everything else, like customer names or shipping addresses, entirely.

["Row storage: great for fetching one full record, wasteful for aggregating one column across millions of rows","Column storage: great for aggregating one or two columns across millions of rows, wasteful for fetching one full record"]
items: Row storage: great for fetching one full record, wasteful for aggregating one column across millions of rows
Column storage: great for aggregating one or two columns across millions of rows, wasteful for fetching one full record

blocks.content: 4.2 Why compression works so well on columns
blocks.text: 4.2 Why compression works so well on columns

blocks.content: Columns also compress far better than rows. A region column might only have twenty distinct values repeated across ten million rows. Storing that column together lets the warehouse compress it aggressively.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396329398-297359888.png
blocks.alt: A column of similar repeated values being compressed into much smaller storage

blocks.content: A row, by contrast, mixes a region code next to a timestamp next to a price, values with very different patterns, which compresses far less efficiently.

blocks.title: Less disk, less I/O, faster scans
blocks.content: Better compression isn't just about saving storage cost. It directly means less data has to move off disk for every query, which is a big part of why OLAP engines can scan millions of rows in seconds.
5. Star schema: fact and dimension tables
blocks.text: 5. Star schema: fact and dimension tables

blocks.content: Once you accept that a warehouse is built for aggregation, the next question is how you model the data inside it. The classic answer is the star schema.
5.1 The fact table
At the center sits a fact table. It records events or transactions, one row per sale, per click, per shipment, whatever the business event is.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396329398-561191804.png
blocks.alt: A central sales fact table surrounded by product, customer, and date dimension tables

blocks.content: A sales fact table typically holds numeric measures, like quantity and amount, plus a set of foreign keys pointing out to the tables that describe the event.
5.2 Dimension tables: who, what, and when
blocks.text: 5.2 Dimension tables: who, what, and when

blocks.content: Surrounding the fact table are dimension tables. Each one describes a different angle on the event: who was involved, what was sold, when it happened, where it happened.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785397016263-381299857.png
blocks.alt: Dimension tables describing customer, product, and date attached to a central fact row

blocks.content: ["Customer dimension answers who","Product dimension answers what","Date dimension answers when","Store or region dimension answers where"]
items: Customer dimension answers who
Product dimension answers what
Date dimension answers when
Store or region dimension answers where

blocks.content: The name star schema comes from the shape: one fact table in the middle, with dimension tables radiating outward like points of a star.
5.3 Worked example: sales fact joined with its dimensions
blocks.text: 5.3 Worked example: sales fact joined with its dimensions

blocks.content: Say the fact table is called fact_sales, with columns like sale_id, product_id, customer_id, date_id, and amount. Around it sit dim_product, dim_customer, and dim_date.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396330979-597884019.png
blocks.alt: Sales fact table joined with product, customer, and date dimensions producing a revenue report

blocks.content: To answer revenue by region last quarter, you join fact_sales to dim_date to filter the quarter, and to dim_customer to bring in the region label to group by.

blocks.title: Reading the join
blocks.text: Every row in fact_sales is one sale. The dimension tables don't multiply the number of rows, they just attach descriptive detail like the product name or the region label onto each sale row.

blocks.content: 6. How data gets into the warehouse
blocks.text: 6. How data gets into the warehouse

blocks.content: A warehouse doesn't magically fill itself. Data has to travel from the production OLTP database into the warehouse on some regular schedule.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396330979-401456864.png
blocks.alt: Production database feeding an extract and transform step that loads into a data warehouse

blocks.content: This movement is handled by ETL or ELT pipelines: extract the data from source systems, transform it into the warehouse's schema, and load it in. There's a dedicated topic on ETL and ELT pipelines that goes deep into how these are built, so this section keeps it brief.
6.1 ETL versus ELT in one line
blocks.text: 6.1 ETL versus ELT in one line

blocks.content: ETL transforms the data before loading it into the warehouse. ELT loads the raw data first and transforms it afterward, usually using the warehouse's own compute power to do the transforming.

{"headers":["ETL","ELT"],"rows":[["Transform happens before loading","Transform happens after loading"],["Warehouse only stores clean, modeled data","Warehouse also stores raw data"],["Classic pattern for on prem warehouses","Common pattern for cloud warehouses like Snowflake and BigQuery"]]}

blocks.title: Batch or streaming
blocks.content: These pipelines can run on a nightly batch schedule or stream continuously. Either way, the warehouse ends up a little behind the live production database, usually by minutes to a day, and that's a completely acceptable tradeoff for analytical work.
7. Real systems you'll run into
Data warehousing isn't just a theoretical pattern. There's a whole industry of products built around exactly this idea.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396330980-859224932.png
blocks.alt: Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, and on premise systems shown as data warehouse choices

blocks.content: ["Snowflake: a cloud warehouse that separates storage from compute, so you can scale each independently","BigQuery: Google's fully managed, serverless warehouse, you mostly just write queries and it handles the infrastructure","Redshift: Amazon's warehouse, tightly integrated with the rest of AWS","Traditional on prem warehouses: older systems like Teradata or Oracle Exadata, still running inside plenty of large enterprises today"]
items: Snowflake: a cloud warehouse that separates storage from compute, so you can scale each independently
BigQuery: Google's fully managed, serverless warehouse, you mostly just write queries and it handles the infrastructure
Redshift: Amazon's warehouse, tightly integrated with the rest of AWS
Traditional on prem warehouses: older systems like Teradata or Oracle Exadata, still running inside plenty of large enterprises today

blocks.content: They all share the same core ideas from this topic: columnar storage, built for OLAP style queries, and fed by ETL or ELT pipelines from operational systems.
8. Worked example: revenue by region last quarter
blocks.text: 8. Worked example: revenue by region last quarter

blocks.content: Let's put the pieces together with an actual query against the star schema from section five.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396330980-779993830.png
blocks.alt: A SQL query aggregating joined sales data into a revenue by region result table

blocks.content:
SELECT
    c.region AS region,
    SUM(f.amount) AS total_revenue
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_customer c ON f.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN dim_date d ON f.date_id = d.date_id
WHERE d.quarter = 'Q2' AND d.year = 2026
GROUP BY c.region
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

code.content:
SELECT
    c.region AS region,
    SUM(f.amount) AS total_revenue
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_customer c ON f.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN dim_date d ON f.date_id = d.date_id
WHERE d.quarter = 'Q2' AND d.year = 2026
GROUP BY c.region
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

codes.sql:
SELECT
    c.region AS region,
    SUM(f.amount) AS total_revenue
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_customer c ON f.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN dim_date d ON f.date_id = d.date_id
WHERE d.quarter = 'Q2' AND d.year = 2026
GROUP BY c.region
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

blocks.content: Walk through what's happening. fact_sales gives every sale. Joining to dim_date narrows it down to just last quarter. Joining to dim_customer brings in the region label. Grouping by region and summing amount gives the final answer.

Notice this query only touches a handful of columns: amount, region, quarter, year. In a columnar warehouse, that means it barely has to read anything from product names, shipping addresses, or the dozen other columns that exist in these tables but aren't part of this question.

blocks.title: This is the columnar payoff in action
blocks.content: This exact query is why columnar storage from section four matters. A row oriented database would have to read full rows, product name, shipping address, everything, just to get at the two or three columns this question actually needs.
9. The interview angle

In a system design interview, data warehousing usually shows up as a follow up, not the main event. You've designed the core operational system, and then the interviewer asks how you'd support analytics or reporting.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396330980-838435506.png
blocks.alt: A decision flow for whether a system design needs a separate data warehouse layer

blocks.content: The signal to listen for is any requirement that sounds like a large aggregate over historical data: dashboards, trends over time, business intelligence, how many, which region, over the last year.

["If the requirement is about a single record right now, that's OLTP. Your existing operational database handles it","If the requirement is about trends, aggregates, or reports across a lot of history, that's OLAP. That's your cue to mention a warehouse layer","A strong answer names the operational database, the warehouse, and the ETL or ELT pipeline that connects them, and explains why running analytics on the operational database directly would be a problem"]
items: If the requirement is about a single record right now, that's OLTP. Your existing operational database handles it
If the requirement is about trends, aggregates, or reports across a lot of history, that's OLAP. That's your cue to mention a warehouse layer

A strong answer names the operational database, the warehouse, and the ETL or ELT pipeline that connects them, and explains why running analytics on the operational database directly would be a problem

blocks.title: Don't over engineer small systems
blocks.content: Not every design needs a warehouse. If the reporting requirement is just show the user their own order history, that's still a small OLTP query. Reach for a warehouse when the scale and shape of the analytical questions genuinely need it.
10. Summary
A data warehouse is a separate, structured store built for analytical queries: OLAP over OLTP, columns over rows, aggregates over single records.

["OLTP handles many small, fast transactional queries for the live application","OLAP handles fewer, much larger analytical queries for reporting and trends","Columnar storage lets OLAP engines read only the columns a query needs, and compress them well","Star schema, a fact table surrounded by dimension tables, is the classic way to model a warehouse","ETL or ELT pipelines move data from production systems into the warehouse on a schedule","Real systems like Snowflake, BigQuery, and Redshift all build on these same ideas"]
items: OLTP handles many small, fast transactional queries for the live application
OLAP handles fewer, much larger analytical queries for reporting and trends
Columnar storage lets OLAP engines read only the columns a query needs, and compress them well
Star schema, a fact table surrounded by dimension tables, is the classic way to model a warehouse
ETL or ELT pipelines move data from production systems into the warehouse on a schedule
Real systems like Snowflake, BigQuery, and Redshift all build on these same ideas

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Analytical queries stay fast and don't touch production","Data in the warehouse is slightly stale, not real time"],["Schema is modeled for reporting, easy to join and aggregate","Extra infrastructure and pipelines to build and maintain"],["Production database stays fast for live users","Another system to monitor, secure, and pay for"]]}

blocks.title: The core tradeoff
blocks.content: You're trading a bit of freshness and some added infrastructure for a system that can answer big analytical questions fast, without ever putting your live application at risk.
